# OSS IQ

> An open-source CLI and MCP server that maps the blast radius of a dependency upgrade in a Python or JavaScript project. It gives you or your coding agent a deterministic, solver-backed update plan. For every package in the dependency graph it reports a next action, version drift, known CVEs and maintenance state.

## What OSS IQ Does

OSS IQ is a Software Composition Analysis (SCA) tool for platform engineers and development teams. It goes beyond vulnerability scanning. Before you change a dependency, it shows what the upgrade moves across the dependency graph. It also shows whether a package is worth depending on at all.

- Scans project manifest files (package.json with package-lock.json; pyproject.toml with uv.lock; pylock.toml; requirements.txt)
- Cross-references against public package registries (npm, PyPI), CVE databases, and GitHub repository signals
- Reports a next action per package, plus a repository-stability verdict (`retain`, `patch`, `refactor` or `evict`) built from exploit probability and upstream maintenance
- Supports JavaScript (npm) and Python (uv, pip lock, pip) ecosystems
- Outputs reports as terminal console, HTML, JSON, or a compact agent format
- Findings never change the exit code; gate CI with your own check over the `ossiq export` JSON

## Commands

Each command answers one question about a dependency, in your terminal or through your coding agent:

- `ossiq status`: What state is my project in? One scan covers every direct and transitive dependency: version drift, known CVEs with their exploit probability, and maintenance health. Each package gets a next action, so you know what to fix first.
- `ossiq info <package>`: Is this package worth depending on? It reports one package inside your project: its version drift, its CVEs and those of its transitive dependencies, and where it sits in your dependency tree. See [Package details](https://ossiq.dev/getting-started.html#package-details).
- `ossiq add <package>`: Is it safe to add right now? A quality gate in front of `npm install` and `uv add`. It shows CVEs, maintainer information and health warnings. After you confirm, it installs the recommended version, not the newest. npm installs run with `--ignore-scripts`. See [Gated package add](https://ossiq.dev/getting-started.html#gated-package-add).
  - Critical warnings block the add unless you pass `--force`. They cover a package its registry has retired or quarantined, a deprecated release you request with `--version`, and a package with a single published version (a common typosquat pattern).
  - A release still inside the cooldown period (7 days by default) gets a warning, not a block.
- `ossiq plan` and `ossiq apply`: What can I upgrade without breaking the tree? The solver simulates the full transitive cascade before it recommends a version. `plan` previews the change and writes nothing. `apply` shows the plan, writes it after you confirm, and rolls back if the install fails. See [Plan and apply updates](https://ossiq.dev/getting-started.html#plan-and-apply-updates).
  - `--update-strategy` sets how far to move: `security`, `deprecation`, `standard` (the default), `latest` or `cutting-edge`.
  - `--strategy-override <package>=<tier>` moves one package differently.
  - `apply --yes` skips the prompt in CI.
- `ossiq install skills`: Can my coding agent do all of this? It installs a skill for Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and GitHub Copilot, and registers a local MCP server for Claude Code and Codex. The agent asks OSS IQ before it adds or updates a dependency. The MCP tools (`ossiq_evaluate_dependency`, `ossiq_evaluate_updates`, `ossiq_update_context`) are read-only: nothing changes until you run `ossiq apply` and confirm. See [Coding agents](https://ossiq.dev/getting-started.html#coding-agents).

## Install and log in

- Run without installing: `uvx ossiq status` (PyPI) or `npx @ossiq/cli status` (npm: a native binary for macOS, Linux glibc and Windows x64; no Python needed)
- Install permanently from PyPI (`uv tool install ossiq` or `pipx install ossiq`), npm (`npm install -g @ossiq/cli`) or Docker (`docker pull ossiq/ossiq-cli`)
- Log in to GitHub once with `ossiq auth login` (one-time code; the token stays in the OS secret store) to raise the API limit from 60 to 5,000 requests per hour. In CI and containers, set `OSSIQ_GITHUB_TOKEN` instead

## Agent benchmark

These figures compare a coding agent that receives an OSS IQ static report with the same agent working unassisted, per dependency update:

- Cost per verified update: $0.164 unassisted, $0.097 with OSS IQ (41% lower)
- Median time: 96 seconds unassisted, 38 seconds with OSS IQ (60% lower)
- Agent turns: 22 unassisted, 8 with OSS IQ
- Registry lookups by the agent: 9 unassisted, 0 with OSS IQ
- Consistency: ten unassisted runs of one upgrade produced two different dependency trees; all ten runs with OSS IQ produced the same one
- Through the MCP server instead of a static report, the saving is 29% on cost and 33% on time

Source: the Round 3 agent benchmark of 28 September 2026, with 60 sessions across two projects and three delivery modes, ten seeds each. Every arm reached 100% verified-correct results, including the unassisted one, so the benchmark makes no claim that OSS IQ improves correctness. Both fixtures have six dependencies and are not production repositories.

## Documentation

- [Getting Started](https://ossiq.dev/getting-started.html): Installation, first scan, and basic usage
- [Log in to GitHub](https://ossiq.dev/how-to/github-login.html): Device-flow login, CI tokens, and troubleshooting
- [Verifying a release](https://ossiq.dev/how-to/verifying-a-release.html): Check the signed SLSA build provenance of an installed artifact with `gh attestation verify`
- [Recommendations and Risk](https://ossiq.dev/recommendations.html): What each recommendation means, the evidence behind it, and what it costs when that evidence is missing or wrong
- [Explanation](https://ossiq.dev/explanation/index.html): How recommendations are made, repository stability, and concepts
- [Reference](https://ossiq.dev/reference.html): Full CLI reference and configuration options
- [Tutorials](https://ossiq.dev/tutorials/): Step-by-step guides for common use cases

## Research & Analysis

- [OSS IQ Journal](https://ossiq.dev/journal/): In-depth reports on software supply chain risk and AI-assisted development
- [The Poisoned Well: How AI Amplifies Open Source Supply Chain Attacks](https://ossiq.dev/journal/the-poisoned-well-ai-supply-chain-attacks.html): Technical synthesis of supply-chain attack patterns, the AI amplification mechanisms (slopsquatting, agentic installs), and a defense-in-depth maturity model
- [The Hidden Cost of AI-Generated Code](https://ossiq.dev/journal/the-hidden-cost-of-ai-generated-code.html): Why faster AI-assisted code writing is degrading code quality, security, and delivery stability

- [npm scan example](https://ossiq.dev/_static/samples/scan_npm.html): Example output for a JavaScript project
- [PyPI scan example](https://ossiq.dev/_static/samples/scan_pypi.html): Example output for a Python project
